title: Courage
hookLine: steady in hard things, neither reckless nor cowardly

lines: FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.
cards: Queen Esther has a problem with a door. Behind it sits the Persian king, and the law says anyone who walks in uncalled is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter.

Her people are about to be destroyed, and she is the one inside the palace. Her cousin Mordecai sends her a message that ends with a question: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
Esther could stay quiet and safe. She could storm in. What she actually does is today's virtue, the one the old Latin lists call fortitude.

teach.b: Fortitude is courage with its feet planted. Christian teachers describe it as a middle path between two failures: the coward who won't face the hard thing, and the reckless one who charges at it without thinking.
Watch Esther walk that path. First, she doesn't rush.
She sends word to Mordecai to gather her people and fast for her, and she and her maids will fast too.
Then she says: "and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." That's not bravado. She's counted the cost and decided.

And when she does walk through the door, she doesn't blurt out the whole crisis. The king holds out the scepter, and she invites him to a banquet. She chooses her moment: courage and prudence, working together.
In the Bible, the call to courage can come with a reason attached.

God tells Joshua, as day 697 heard: "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." The courage isn't self-made.
It rests on not being alone.

teach.h: POWER, LOVE, AND A SOUND MIND.
teach.b: And Paul writes to Timothy: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." Power and a sound mind, side by side. Steady, not wild.
Jews read Esther's story aloud at Purim, and some Christians read it as a picture of a frightened person who walks through the door anyway.

how: Christian moral teaching names fortitude among the cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Spirit in Catholic teaching; some Christians pray for courage before hard tasks, and the story of Esther is read in churches and at the Jewish festival of Purim.

games.q: you're Esther. your people are in danger, and going to the king uncalled could cost your life. what do you do?
o: stay quiet; you might be spared.
ask your people to fast with you, then go in, whatever the cost.
storm in at once and denounce the plot.
games.why: she prepares, then goes: "and if I perish, I perish." and once inside, she invites the king to a banquet and picks her moment.

practice: Name something you've been avoiding because it scares you a little, a phone call, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, and instead of solving it, do what Esther did first: get still, and prepare.
Plant your feet on the floor and picture yourself doing it calmly. If you pray, you can hold Joshua's words: be strong and of a good courage.

wordCard.voice: Fortitude. Steady courage in hard things: neither running from them nor charging in blind. One of the cardinal virtues.

orig.note: Latin: strength, steadiness; the name Latin-speaking Christian teachers gave this virtue.

carryVoice: Your line: steady courage. Esther went in not knowing how it would end. Back tomorrow, same hill.
